processing: Fully oxidised black tea made both as orthodox whole and broken leaf and as CTC, the machine-cut granules used for strong, quick brews.
harvest_season: Sold through the year; as with other Assam gardens, the May to June second flush is generally the most sought after.
appearance_dry: Orthodox grades are dark with golden tips; CTC is small, even, dark granules.
appearance_liquor: Deep reddish brown, darker and quicker to colour in the CTC.
appearance_wet: Coppery leaf in orthodox grades; fine dark-copper particles in CTC.
taste_profile: Typical of a strong Upper Assam: malty and full-bodied, brisk in the CTC and rounder in the tippy orthodox lots.

brewing.notes: Timing depends on the grade: CTC needs only about two minutes, tippy orthodox three to four. CTC is the natural choice for milk tea.

vintage_note: Sold by year, flush and grade, with both CTC and orthodox offered through the year. As usual for Assam, buy the most recent season and drink it within a year or two; second-flush orthodox lots are the ones sellers label by flush.
description:
Halmari is an Upper Assam garden in the Moran area, owned by the Daga family and covering 374 hectares. Tea specialists often list it among the better-known estates of the region, and its name reaches shoppers well beyond India.

It makes two quite different teas: orthodox leaf and CTC. Orthodox keeps visible leaf and tip, while CTC is cut into granules that release colour and strength within a couple of minutes.

Pick the grade for how you drink. CTC suits a milky, sturdy cup or a pot of chai; tippy orthodox grades are better tried plain first, where the malt and any sweetness are easier to notice. As with other Assam teas, long steeps push them towards bitterness.

The label should say grade and flush. A broad range is on sale under this one name, so two Halmari packs can taste like entirely different teas.
history: The estate is described as having operated for over a century, though no founding year or founder is reliably recorded in accessible accounts. Its modern reputation rests on the Daga family's ownership and on a trade serving both Indian and foreign buyers, including hotels.
